payload.throughline: Read the boundary, permeability, gradient, energy source, and coordination function before predicting movement or selecting a membrane structure.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes check: match a membrane component to containment, transport, fluidity, or coating. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.
Amphipathic phospholipids form a bilayer; proteins provide specialized routes and signals; cholesterol is a steroid fluidity modifier; waxes form protective coatings rather than the main bilayer.
Polar heads face water and nonpolar tails form a hydrophobic core that selectively contains aqueous compartments.
Many lipids and proteins move laterally, creating a dynamic fluid mosaic; cholesterol buffers phospholipid packing.
Picture a self-sealing two-sided oil layer with movable specialist components.
I choose the bilayer for baseline containment, a protein for one selective route, cholesterol for temperature-dependent fluidity, and wax for an external coating.
A charged solute is retained by the hydrophobic core unless a carrier is present.
Reduced cholesterol at low temperature permits tighter phospholipid packing and less fluidity buffering.
Identify the function, then select the component that directly performs it.
Use boundary material versus specialist component.
Explain a fresh membrane feature independently.
Waxes protect surfaces but are not the main plasma-membrane bilayer; the fluid mosaic is not a rigid lattice.
Near exit: identify the source of selective containment.
Changed exit: predict a qualitative cholesterol-fluidity effect.
Repair containment by tracing heads, tails, core polarity, and solute charge.
Freshly reapply the containment model to a new ion.
Repair dynamics by separating bilayer structure from cholesterol regulation.
Freshly reapply cholesterol buffering under a new temperature condition.
Phospholipids contain, proteins specialize, cholesterol tunes fluidity, and waxes coat.
Low-stakes check: identify the moving species, permeability, gradient, and energy use. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.
Passive transport moves down an electrochemical gradient without direct energy; osmosis is net water movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
Simple diffusion crosses the lipid region directly; facilitated diffusion uses a protein but remains downhill.
Water shifts toward greater effective nonpenetrating-solute concentration; ideal osmotic pressure rises with effective particle concentration at fixed temperature.
Use a gate-and-gradient map: who can cross, which way is downhill, and which particles remain to sustain water movement.
I do not count total solute until I check permeability. A permeant solute can equilibrate; a nonpenetrating solute sustains the osmotic difference.
A carrier moves a polar solute downhill without ATP: facilitated diffusion.
More nonpenetrating particles at equal temperature produce greater ideal osmotic pressure.
Mark permeability and gradient before naming the process.
Use direct crossing, protein-assisted downhill movement, or water movement.
Predict a fresh passive movement independently.
A protein route does not automatically mean active transport; direct energy or uphill coupling is required.
Near exit: predict water direction from nonpenetrating solute.
Changed exit: relate particle concentration to osmotic pressure.
Repair osmosis by identifying water permeability and nonpenetrating particles.
Freshly predict water movement with a new nonpenetrating solute.
Repair the colligative relation by comparing effective particle counts.
Freshly compare equal particle concentrations with different solute identities.
Permeability decides what crosses; gradients set passive direction; nonpenetrating particle count sets osmotic drive.
Low-stakes check: separate energy-driven pumps from passive channels. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.
Pumps use energy to maintain gradients; channels permit passive ion movement down electrochemical gradients; charge movement changes membrane potential.
The sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in per ATP, helping maintain ion gradients.
Net positive entry makes the interior less negative; net positive exit or negative entry makes it more negative.
Pumps charge the gradient battery; channels open a path for the battery to discharge.
I first determine pump or channel, then the net electrochemical direction, then the sign of charge movement and voltage change.
ATP-driven uphill sodium export is active transport.
Sodium entry through a channel usually makes the interior less negative.
Mark energy, gradient direction, ion sign, and movement.
Use pump versus pore, then charge direction.
Predict a fresh ion movement independently.
A channel does not pump ions uphill, and a pump is not simply an always-open pore.
Near exit: classify an ATP-driven uphill movement.
Changed exit: convert channel-mediated charge movement into voltage direction.
Repair transport by pairing direct energy with uphill movement.
Freshly classify a new ATP-driven ion movement.
Repair voltage by tracking the sign and direction of net charge.
Freshly predict voltage after negative-charge entry.
Pumps maintain gradients; channels follow them; net charge movement determines potential direction.
Low-stakes check: match signal, vesicle, direct communication, seal, or adhesion to its membrane structure. It neither selects a route nor awards exit credit.
Receptors detect extracellular signals; endocytosis and exocytosis move cargo by vesicles; gap, tight, and desmosomal junctions coordinate neighboring cells in different ways.
Endocytosis moves membrane and cargo inward; exocytosis fuses a vesicle outward.
Gap junctions pass small molecules directly, tight junctions seal between cells, and desmosomes resist mechanical stress.
Use five verbs: detect, internalize/release, communicate, seal, and anchor.
I select by function, not by cell type: ligand detection means receptor; paracellular leak means tight junction; pulling failure means desmosome.
Vesicle fusion releasing protein is exocytosis.
Loss of a between-cell seal with intact membranes points to tight-junction failure.
Name the failed function before selecting the structure.
Use detect, traffic, communicate, seal, or anchor.
Select a fresh membrane coordination structure independently.
Gap junctions communicate but do not seal; tight junctions seal but do not provide tensile anchoring; desmosomes anchor but do not form communication pores.
Near exit: identify receptor-mediated surface signaling.
Changed exit: identify a paracellular sealing failure.
Repair signaling by tracing ligand binding to intracellular response.
Freshly identify a surface receptor with a new ligand.
Repair junction selection by separating seal from adhesion and communication.
Freshly identify mechanical-adhesion failure with an intact seal.
Receptors detect, vesicles traffic, gap junctions communicate, tight junctions seal, and desmosomes anchor.

question_evidence_plan.changed_dimension_detail: Changes from containment to cholesterol-mediated dynamics.
Changes temperature condition while preserving cholesterol buffering.
Changes from water-direction prediction to a colligative pressure comparison.
Changes solute identity while holding effective particle concentration fixed.
Changes from pump/channel classification to charge-to-voltage prediction.
Changes ion sign while preserving charge accounting.
Changes from receptor signaling to a paracellular sealing failure.
Changes from sealing failure to mechanical adhesion failure while preserving junction selection.
